result.summary: Pausanias opens Book 6 by explaining that he will describe only the more renowned or finer statues of Olympic victors. He then walks past statues near the temple of Hera, noting wrestlers, boxers, horse-race winners, Cynisca's chariot group, and Spartan chariot victors.

scenes.title: Principles for choosing statues
scenes.summary: Pausanias explains that not every victor has a statue and that he will mention only the most renowned or finest.

scenes.title: Statues beside the temple of Hera
scenes.summary: Statues of wrestlers, boxers and horse-race winners from Elis and elsewhere are listed with their sculptors, including Troilus's controversial win and the dream of Dinolochus's mother.

scenes.title: Cynisca and the Spartan victors
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the chariot group of Cynisca and the statues of Spartan victors Anaxander and Polycles.

alias_notes.explanation: A surname of Polycles, meaning roughly 'much bronze'.

notable_quotes.reason: Pausanias states his method: a record of statues and offerings, not a list of victors.

analysis.text: Pausanias is selective, favouring renown and artistry over completeness, and ties victories to sculptors and local pride.
Cynisca's statue shows that a woman could win Olympic chariot victories as an owner, since owners rather than drivers were crowned.

fun_facts.text: Olympic victors' crowns were of wild olive, as this chapter notes.

language_notes.text: "Amateurs" here likely means private individuals, not professional athletes, who competed or owned entrants; the sense is a little loose in this translation.
The crown of wild olive was the Olympic victor's prize, cut from a sacred tree at Olympia.
"Stud" means a breeding stable of horses; Cleogenes won with a horse he himself had bred.
"Umpire" translates the Greek Hellanodikes, the Elean judges of the games; Troilus held this office when he won.
"Proclaimed" refers to the herald announcing the victor's name aloud, the formal act of declaring a win.
The pentathlum (pentathlon) was a five-event contest: running, jumping, discus, javelin and wrestling.
"Polychalcus" means roughly "much bronze"; a riband is a fillet or ribbon tied on victors.
The Pythian, Isthmian and Nemean games, with Olympia, formed the four great Greek festival circuits.

context_notes.text: The temple of Hera at Olympia was one of the oldest buildings in the sanctuary, and statues stood around it.
The Eleans managed the games, so the rule was a reform responding to a perceived conflict of interest.
Lysippus of Sicyon was a famous fourth-century BC bronze sculptor, known as Alexander's court sculptor.
Cynisca, a Spartan princess and daughter of King Archidamus, was the first woman to win an Olympic victory, with horses she owned.

literary_notes.text: Pausanias speaks as a selective, judging guide, explaining his criteria of renown and artistic quality to the reader.
The mother's dream of embracing her crowned son anticipates his victory, presenting the win as divinely signaled.
The small details of the two boys, one with the wheel and one begging the riband, give the statue group a lively, human scene.
